title: CHAPTER ELEVEN. On the immutability of God; definition
english: CHAPTER ELEVEN. On the immutability of God.

Thus far there has been the third attribute of God, namely simplicity: there follows the fourth, namely immutability, which is God's highest perfection, by which He always remains the same as He isIMMUTABILITY, which certain Greeks render as unchangeableness, is expressed from the sacred letters not by a distinct word, but by like and opposite words of power.

title: Scriptural vocabulary of immutability; formal ratio
english: It is of like power that of God it is affirmed in Psalm 102:27, But You remain. And in verse 28, But You are the same. And Malachi 3:6, I do not change. So Romans 1:23 says the incorruptible God. 1 Timothy 6:16, who alone has immortality. Opposite words of power are denied of Him in James 1:17: with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.

The material in this attribute also is the same as in the rest, namely God's most eminent perfection. But its formal ratio consists in the negation of every change by which God in His essence would become other and other. For He never acquires a new perfection, nor loses that which He possesses.

title: Proofs 1-4: unity, necessity, infinity, simplicity
english: That God is in Himself plainly immutable I show in this way. FIRST, from His most eminent unity. Whatever is most eminently one is in itself plainly immutable. But God is most eminently one, as was demonstrated in chapter IV of this book. Therefore God is in Himself plainly immutable.

SECOND, from the absolute necessity of existing. Whatever exists by absolute necessity is in itself plainly immutable. But God exists by absolute necessity, as was demonstrated in chapter VIII. THIRD, from the infinite perfection of essence. Whatever is endowed with infinite perfection is in itself plainly immutable. FOURTH, from simplicity. Whatever is absolutely simple is in itself plainly immutable, because it is capable of no accident. But God is absolutely simple, as was demonstrated in chapter X.

title: Proofs 5-8: modes of change; independence; potency; first mover
english: FIFTH, from an induction of the modes by which an intelligent nature can be changed: as to existence; as to accidents; as to knowledge; as to decree or purpose of will. But by none of these modes is God changed. SIXTH, from independence. Whoever is independent is plainly immutable in Himself. But God is independent, as was proved in chapter V.

SEVENTH, from the state of a being in potency. Whatever is mutable is somehow in potency. But God is in no way in potency. Pure act, indeed the purest, is God alone. EIGHTH, from the nature of motion. That from which every motion and change is, is simply immobile and immutable, as Augustine and Boethius assert from Aristotle. But from God is every motion and change.

title: Against Vorstius; five scholastic objections deferred
english: Conrad Vorstius in his Notes on Disputation III On God seems somehow to deny this attribute of God, writing that the fifth species of change can have a place in God insofar as He exercises certain immanent actions according to free will.

But of old certain doubts were objected to the orthodox consensus by the scholastics: first, that God began to act; second, that yesterday He knew the sun would rise today; third, that His liberty would be taken away if He could not change His will; fourth, that He was made man; fifth, that God was changed because He suffered and died. Each of these arguments has its proper seat below. Meanwhile, since it is certain that God is entirely immutable and immobile, a few rules are here to be observed, useful for solving contrary arguments.

title: Rules 1-8 on change, motion, and relations
english: RULES. 1. Change properly is according to substance, but motion according to accident. Hence, since God is in potency neither in substance nor in accidental forms, He is altogether immutable. 2. God is said to move Himself by an effect of nature, or of grace, or of glory; such motion is not referred to God, but to His effect. 3. God governs the world by a motion which is from Him, not which is in Him; the preposition in, when He is called unchangeable, does not deprive Him of active power of moving, but denies passive power of being moved.

4. Motions of approach and withdrawal are not referred to God except according to effect. 5. God does not now hold Himself otherwise than from eternity; He is called creator and conserver by a relation that denominates Him only extrinsically. 6. From habit to act only those are changed which so act that they can suffer. 7. When God is said now to will what He did not will before, that says a change in the thing willed, not in the one willing. 8. The ratio of personal relation in the divine is other than that of other relations in creatures.

title: Rules 9-16; pastoral uses — Cap. 11 COMPLETE
english: 9. God is always the same because of His essence, intellect, will, and power, as stated in Psalm 102:27-28. 10. God repents, not because He changes counsels, but benefits and judgments, as He decreed to change them. 11. What God under condition decrees, commands, promises, threatens, or does, argues His liberty, goodness, or severity, not mutability. 12. God does not depend on creatures, but decrees that He will do something through creatures and about them.

13. God, by creating, redeeming, and doing other things outside Himself, is not changed, but freely applies His omnipotence, clemency, and justice to various objects. 14. God from angry becomes placated and vice versa, not by change of essence, but by exchange of judgment with benefit. 15. Prayers, holiness, and evil life do not change God, but the works of God according to His decree. 16. The immutability of God serves faith, lest we take for God what changes; consolation, that we may be persuaded God will never change His goodwill toward us; and piety, that we too may be constant and immutable in the love of God and neighbor.
